items.title: Ten human Sikh Gurus, then the eternal Guru Granth Sahib
items.claim: How does the Sikh tradition handle leadership after Guru Gobind Singh?

options.text: It ended with the tenth Guru with no continuation
In 1708 Guru Gobind Singh declared the Guru Granth Sahib (the scripture) to be the eternal Guru — no further human gurus
It continues through a hereditary line

items.reveal:
Guru Gobind Singh died in 1708 from a stab wound inflicted by an Afghan assassin. Before his death he installed the Adi Granth (compiled by Guru Arjan in 1604) as Guru Granth Sahib — making the scripture the eternal Guru.

The Guru Granth Sahib (1,430 pages, mostly in Gurmukhi script) contains hymns by six of the ten Gurus, plus 15 Hindu and Muslim saints (bhagats) — including Kabir and Sheikh Farid. It is treated as a living Guru: bowed to, awakened in the morning, put to rest at night.

Sikh gurdwaras place the Guru Granth Sahib on a throne (palki) as the central focus.
items.why: The structural innovation of designating scripture as eternal Guru ended succession disputes that plague many religions. Sikh community continuity rests on the text, not on a living hierarchy.

items.title: The Hebrew Bible barely mentions an afterlife
items.claim: What does the Hebrew Bible (the Christian Old Testament) say about heaven and hell?

options.text: It describes both in detail throughout
It mostly speaks of Sheol — a shadowy underworld where the dead exist as shades — with explicit resurrection only in late texts like Daniel 12

items.reveal:
Job 3:13-19, Ecclesiastes 9:5-10 ('the dead know nothing') and the Psalms describe Sheol as a silent underworld common to all the dead. Daniel 12:2 (mid-2nd century BCE) is the clearest explicit resurrection passage — and it's one of the latest books.

By Jesus's time, Pharisees believed in resurrection and Sadducees did not (Mark 12:18-27). Christian heaven and hell as detailed afterlife destinations are largely shaped by intertestamental Jewish apocalyptic literature, Greek thought and later Christian elaboration (Dante most famously).
items.why: Students often assume the afterlife is a 'religious universal'. Within the Abrahamic tradition itself it's a developing idea, with the most familiar version being relatively recent.

items.title: Muslims believe the Quran was revealed via the angel Gabriel
items.claim: How do Muslims understand the Quran's origin?

options.text: Muhammad's wise sayings, gathered over centuries
The direct word of God, revealed to Muhammad through the angel Jibril (Gabriel) over 23 years (610-632 CE), to be recited and transmitted unchanged in Arabic
A revised version of the Bible adapted for Arabia

items.reveal:
The word 'Quran' comes from the Arabic root q-r-' meaning 'to recite'. The first revelation (Sura 96, 'Iqra' — 'Recite!') is dated to around 610 CE at the Cave of Hira on Mount Jabal al-Nour.

The Quran was compiled in written form under the third caliph Uthman (around 650 CE), with non-conforming versions destroyed to ensure a single authoritative text. Muslims regard only the Arabic text as the Quran proper; translations are 'meanings of' the Quran.

The Hadith — sayings of Muhammad — is a separate category, compiled by his companions and successors. Major Sunni collections: Sahih al-Bukhari (d. 870) and Sahih Muslim (d. 875).
items.why: The Quran's status differs from how Christians understand the Bible. Islamic theology treats every Arabic word as direct divine speech — which is why translation is always 'the meaning of' rather than 'the Quran'.
